text:
Norman Swan: Hello, welcome to this week's edition of the Health Report with
me, Norman Swan. Today, time for a cold shower on the hype around medicinal
cannabis. Could Mars Bars protect against obesity? How obesity might not be
the main step on the road to diabetes. And the prospect that a blood test could
tell you as much about your cancer as a biopsy.

There's been a remarkable turnaround in attitudes and legislation making it
easier for people to take cannabis for medicinal purposes, and for the
manufacture of cannabis products for medical uses. But before we get carried
away, an editorial in this week's Medical Journal of Australia warns that there are
still significant gaps in knowledge which could put users at risk. One of the co-
authors of the editorial is Jennifer Martin, who is Professor of Clinical
Pharmacology at the University of Newcastle, and Jennifer was in our Newcastle
studio last night. Welcome to the Health Report.

Jennifer Martin: Thank you, I'm pleased to be here.

Norman Swan: You talk about that you still require data…we still don't know how
effective, how safe and what the dose range is of these cannabis products.

Jennifer Martin: That's correct. We need more data, but in addition we also
need a whole lot of other things to happen to make sure that we have actually
ensured that patients are safe when they take cannabis.

Norman Swan: So what are the worries? Are there any signals about worries at
the moment?

Jennifer Martin: I think there are a lot of concerns from prescribers, for example
they have concerns as to how they would write a script for cannabis, which type
of cannabis would they prescribe, how would they prefer to give it? Is it given in a
tablet or vaporised or smoked? What is the recommendation for this particular
patient with this particular disease? So I think there are concerns in the
profession about that aspect. I also think there are concerns in other areas that
maybe haven't had so much coverage such as the pharmacists who are going to
have to be sure they know how to store the cannabis and that all of the many
different cannabis products…they'll have to know how to look after them, what
the security is around them, how these things will be prescribed and what the
follow-up for patients is.
 
Norman Swan: Are there many products on the market yet? What's around at
the moment in Australia? I know there is a lot on the market in the United States.

Jennifer Martin: Yes, so it's still an illegal substance, that's the law. But patients
that I look after in the hospital are still able to access different types of cannabis
and cannabinoid from overseas, and many grow it actually at home in the Hunter
and make up their own products. So there is quite a market out there of people
that are already making or importing these therapeutic products to use
themselves medicinally.

Norman Swan: Have you seen anybody get into strife?

Jennifer Martin: I have actually seen quite a few people in strife. Most of them
actually it's after the event and we are talking about how to manage, for example,
their end-stage heart failure or their end-stage airways disease, and they tell me
about a bad experience they've had with cannabis that has been
prescribed…well, it's not prescribed, that has been brought to them by friends or
family members that are trying to be helpful. And these are a particular
population group that is often neglected in health, such as the elderly, and the
elderly patients, they describe quite significant cognitive and dysphoric reactions
after having cannabis.

Norman Swan: And if you are importing cannabis from overseas, do we know
what's in it?

Jennifer Martin: We don't know what's in it, that's correct. There are places that
you can get it tested. For example, at Newcastle University we have the facilities
to actually identify compounds that are actually within the cannabinoid product.
Most of them are THC, which is the hallucinogenic compound, and CBD which is
a cannabidiol which has been studied in epilepsy, but there are a variety of other
things that are in there and that are added to it. But that's correct, people
themselves actually wouldn't know that.

Norman Swan: Some people would say (and I can just see my mailbag
tomorrow morning), well, you know, these are just the old farts in the medical
profession trying to put up the barriers here and the best thing is just to smoke it,
all this medicinal stuff is just a smokescreen for pharmaceutical companies to
make a lot of money.
 
Jennifer Martin: Yes, that's exactly the feedback we get from some members of
the community as well, they are a bit frustrated that the trials are taking so long.
We haven't even started recruiting for some of them. We don't have an active
pharmacovigilance program out there, and people are saying, well, why are you
taking so long, we all know the stuff is good, why don't you just get on with it?
And I think for recreational users that's a reasonable argument because we do
have 2,000 years of information from people who use it recreationally.

But medicinal cannabis is used in a completely different group usually, it's usually
an older group, they are usually pretty frail and comorbid, that means they have
lots of other medical problems. They are on lots and lots of drugs that might
interact with the cannabis, they might have difficulty inhaling a particular form of
cannabis because they lack the ability to inhale to get the active ingredients.

So I think the group that we're getting a lot of pressure from is usually a
recreational group, and I think that what I'm concerned about as a medical
practitioner is more about protecting patients, about making sure we actually
don't give them something that's not safe and actually potentially harm them. I
actually think that's a reasonable…I mean, I understand what you're saying about
the paternalistic…well, potentially implying that this might be the paternalistic
view of medicine, but I do think we have a duty to protect patients as well. And
the other point I have is just that there is a bit of research to suggest that some of
these molecules in the cannabis are actually quite helpful, and if we get it wrong,
if we actually don't do the studies properly upfront and choose the wrong dose to
study, then we might think…

Norman Swan: You could spoil it.

Jennifer Martin: We could spoil it, and you never get a second chance to go
back on that, the energy is gone and people are onto something else. So I think it
was really not trying to be…

Norman Swan: So go slower to get it right.

Jennifer Martin: I think so, and put the time and investment upfront to do the
studies properly.

Norman Swan: Jennifer, thanks very much for joining us.
 
Jennifer Martin: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Jennifer Martin is Professor of Clinical Pharmacology at the
University of Newcastle.

And you're listening to the Health Report here on RN with me, Norman Swan.

Research published by Australian researchers in a prestigious international
journal could be interpreted as showing that eating confectionery protects against
obesity. Before you scream with delight and devour that bar of chocolate you've
been eyeing in the cupboard, there may be more to this story. Earlier today I
spoke to two of the authors from the Murdoch Children's Research Institute in
Melbourne, Constantine Gasser and Professor Melissa Wake.

Melissa, what's the context for this study?

Melissa Wake: We've been very interested in obesity for a long time, and I think
it is becoming fairly clear that we have kind of hit a wall. So after 15 years of
really trying with education and lifestyle advice et cetera, we haven't got very far.
And we really felt that we needed to go back a little bit and really start to try and
unpick some possible contributors to obesity and healthy weight. So that led to
Constantine looking at this under-researched area.

Norman Swan: Which is the influence of confectionery on obesity. So what did
you do, Constantine?

Constantine Gasser: We conducted a systematic review where we combined
the results of 19 studies from around the world to look at the association between
confectionery consumption and overweight and obesity in children and
adolescents.

Norman Swan: Confectionery defined as what?

Constantine Gasser: Candy and chocolates, but not including other types of
sweets and deserts. So we looked at confectionery and overweight and obesity
and found to our surprise people with higher intakes of confectionery were
actually slightly less likely to be overweight or obese.

Norman Swan: Where the studies consistently in that direction?
 
Constantine Gasser: So most of the studies were consistently in that direction.

Norman Swan: So it's absolutely counterintuitive. And before we jump to the
conclusion that we should all go out and chomp away at a Mars Bar to protect
ourselves against obesity, let's just assume a neutral position for the moment on
this finding. If the finding were to be real, what sort of risk reduction on obesity
did you get for confectionery use?

Constantine Gasser: We compared children in the highest versus the lowest to
our reference category of confectionery consumption in the studies, and this
differed across each of the studies, but we found that overall the odds or
likelihood of being overweight or obese was approximately 20% lower for
children in the highest compared to the lowest or a reference category of
consumption, and this was similar for both chocolate and non-chocolate
confectionery.

Norman Swan: So, Constantine, I can hear people rejoicing across the land. Do
you think the finding is real? Given that several studies have shown it and if we
were talking about a more neutral topic you'd have said, oh, this is it, signed,
sealed and delivered, factor X protects you against Y, no problem at all.

Constantine Gasser: Well, we think that there are a number of possible reasons
for these findings. Firstly, the possibilities that confectionery may be a small
aspect of the diet of these children and adolescents, so it may not be contributing
very much to their daily energy or sugar intake. For example, US data shows that
confectionery or candy in the US comprises approximately 5% of their sugar
intake compared to soft drinks and other sugar sweetened drinks, which
comprise approximately 30%.

However, another reason for these findings is that overweight or obese children
or adolescents or their parents may reduce their confectionery intake if they
believe that it's an easy target in order to combat overweight or obesity, so they
may be reducing their intake of these foods.

Norman Swan: So what you're saying here is obese people have artificially
lowered their confectionery rates to try and control their obesity, and therefore
people who are thinner look artificially as if they are in a higher group.
 
Constantine Gasser: Yes, or they may have also underreported their intake of
confectionery if they believe that it was socially desirable to be consuming less
confectionery for health outcomes such as obesity, and as a result this may have
been an explanation for some of the findings as well.

Norman Swan: But it also could be real, that once you've had a lolly or two or a
bit of chocolate, your appetite for other sugar and other high calorie foods is
lower, and therefore there is a trade-off which is beneficial.

Constantine Gasser: Yes, possibly because of sugar being lower in kilojoules
than fat, then this may have also been another possible explanation, meaning
that they may have had an increased sense of fullness and consumed less of
other foods. But we do need to also consider the quantities that are being
consumed and also the detrimental effect of confectionery on other health
outcomes such as tooth decay, for example because of the high sugar content.
So we are certainly not saying that we should be encouraging high intakes of
confectionery.

Norman Swan: So Melissa Wake, you were hoping to illuminate the literature on
obesity and diet, and all you succeeded in doing is confusing it even more.

Melissa Wake: Well, we think that we have come up with a really interesting
finding. It does seem likely that confectionery consumption is a fairly small part of
children's food intake today. We think that the culprits for obesity are likely to be
too much food, so large servings, uncontrolled snacks, second helpings et
cetera, and also the sorts of foods that kids are predominantly eating; sugary
drinks, but also foods that are high in fat and salt and sugar and processed
carbohydrates, and large in terms of portion size.

Norman Swan: So Health Report listeners across the land and indeed across
the world since we've got Canadian listeners, are looking in their cupboard
hungrily at that bar of chocolate. What should they do with it, Melissa?

Melissa Wake: Well, first they should make sure that it's dark chocolate. They
should encourage children to eat sparingly. Certainly we know that dark
chocolate does actually have some health benefits. It does increase satiety, it's
quite hard to overindulge in dark chocolate, and its high flavonoid content has
been shown to have health benefits such as lower blood pressure. So I would
 
say keep an open mind, eat sparingly, and if your child does eat confectionery,
steer them towards something that does have ancillary health benefits.

Norman Swan: Thank you both very much indeed for joining us on the Health
Report.

Melissa Wake: It's a pleasure.

Constantine Gasser: Thanks Norman.

Norman Swan: Melissa Wake and Constantine Gasser at the Murdoch
Children's Research Institute in Melbourne.

Speaking of sugar and obesity, there are about a million people with diabetes in
Australia, which includes around 130,000 with what's called type 1, that's the
insulin-dependent form and not related to obesity necessarily. We are among the
highest prevalence nations in the world, and one of the problems with diabetes
that doesn't get much attention is the risk of hypoglycaemia, dangerously low
levels of blood sugar. And worryingly, some people with diabetes lose their ability
to recognise when their blood sugar is plummeting. And one answer may be re-
teaching people to become scared.

A world authority on hypoglycaemia was in Melbourne a few days ago, which is
where I caught up with her. And as you'll also hear, Professor Stephanie Amiel of
Kings College London also has fascinating findings on which comes first in type 2
diabetes; obesity or problems with insulin. And also, surprising side-effects of
obesity surgery. But let's start with hypoglycaemia.

Stephanie Amiel: A hypoglycaemic attack is never pleasant. For most people
they are what we call mild, but the patient may not feel them as mild because
what happens is the blood sugar goes low, they have a stress response which is
symptomatic, so it feels unpleasant, but they also know what is happening so
they eat something and it stops. The problem is that sometimes, particularly in
people who have lost the ability to feel that hypoglycaemia like that, the first thing
that happens is confusion and cognitive impairment, so they never get the
opportunity to treat themselves, the blood glucose goes on falling, they become
confused, they may behave in an embarrassing or abnormal way, and they may
 
get into loss of consciousness and seizure. And so those severe hypoglycaemic
attacks are obviously really very distressing and very unpleasant.

Norman Swan: And that's what you are trying to prevent. If you've got lack of
awareness, there is a major issue.

Stephanie Amiel: Yes, if you have too many minor hypos, most people will then
lose their ability to recognise them, and therefore they are much more prone to
get a more severe hypo. So if you've got type 1 diabetes and you don't recognise
when your blood glucose dips below, let's say, about three millimole per litre…

Norman Swan: And just to give people a sense of that, you've got diabetes when
you're fasting blood sugar is at seven, so three is at the lower end.

Stephanie Amiel: Sure, so under three and people start to notice or other people
start to notice in them a slight slowing of brain function. And so if you are not
noticing your own hypoglycaemia at or around that sort of level, then your risk for
having one of these more severe episodes is much increased. And if you are a
type 1 diabetic, so totally insulin-dependent from the beginning, then not being
aware of your hypoglycaemia increases your risk of having a really bad episode
by about sixfold. And if you are on insulin and you are type 2 diabetic person,
then 17-fold. It's a big risk factor.

Norman Swan: That's huge.

Stephanie Amiel: It is huge.

Norman Swan: You've been working on how you restore that awareness.

Stephanie Amiel: Yes, for a long time. It's time we got there! You can restore
it…this is going to sound very circular, but you can restore it by avoiding
exposure to a plasma glucose or blood glucose of under three because basically
what happens is the brain gets used to whatever you show it. So if you show it a
lot of blood glucoses of under three it stops noticing and stops warning you about
it.

Norman Swan: And that can happen to people who are trying too hard to keep
their blood sugar down.
 
Stephanie Amiel: Yes, it can, and particularly people who are very, very
committed to being really tightly controlled. And healthcare professionals have
been very good at telling people what glucose level they should be under. We
haven't been so good at making sure they realise that there is also a lower limit
to normality which they should remain over.

Norman Swan: So how do you get people to put a stop?

Stephanie Amiel: The most successful thing is to train people to manage their
own insulin very physiologically, so we call it flexible intensified insulin therapy,
and that's usually successful, so that will restore awareness of hypoglycaemia to
just under half of people who have lost awareness, and it hugely reduces the risk
of severe hypoglycaemia in the type 1 diabetic population.

Norman Swan: And in the Type 2?

Stephanie Amiel: We haven't done so much in the Type 2 because it's not such
a big problem for the type 2s, and that's partly because most Type 2s, even when
they need insulin, do still have a bit of their own insulin, and it seems to be all
they need to protect themselves from severe hypoglycaemia. Also partly because
there are now used agents, new non-insulin agents available for people that don't
carry the same hypoglycaemia risk. So if someone with Type 2 is having
hypoglycaemia problems, it's usually a matter of changing them onto one of
these in newer therapies with lower hypoglycaemic potential. And if they are on
insulin, then their problems are the same as the type 1s and they can join that
program.

Norman Swan: And it has also been found that transplanting part of the
pancreas can help too, and also you've been looking at psychological therapies.

Stephanie Amiel: Yes, there is one step in between that which is the use of the
newer technologies of glucose sensing and insulin delivery…

Norman Swan: These are the pumps and so on.

Stephanie Amiel: Sure. Because transplantation, it works but it's obviously not
suitable for everybody, and it's certainly not available to everybody.
 
We've been looking at psychological issues for a variety of reasons. We looked
at the brain's response to hypoglycaemia in a very scientific way, we did brain
imaging, brain scanning, and found that people who were unaware of their
hypoglycaemia had very different brain responses to hypoglycaemia, including a
failure to generate a message to themselves that this was something really
unpleasant that they should avoid at all costs.

Norman Swan: So they had a low stress response?

Stephanie Amiel: They had a low stress response, so they didn't have the stress
response, they didn't have the symptoms, we expected that because they were
unaware, what we didn't expect was they had different responses of the brain
areas that tell us we are having fun, the reward areas. And instead of turning
those off and really knowing that this was unpleasant, they weren't doing that and
some of them were even activating those areas in the opposite direction.

Norman Swan: Is that because of the sort of person they were or because of the
diabetes?

Stephanie Amiel: That's an extremely good question. We are testing that at the
moment. We think it's just part of the whole syndrome of having induced a
tolerance, if you like, of hypoglycaemia because you've been exposed to it too
often. But it is possible that this particular part of the response in what we call the
frontal areas of the brain, that might be genetically programmed in an individual,
so it may be that these people are programmed to respond to a stress in a
particular way that makes them more vulnerable to developing this whole
problem of unawareness.

Norman Swan: So teach them to become scared.

Stephanie Amiel: Absolutely we need to teach them to become scared because
if you don't feel something it's not surprising that you don't worry about it. But if
we can teach them to become scared, they will then be able to access all the
other information they've been given that they should have been able to use
before to help them avoid hypoglycaemia.
 
Norman Swan: Now, your group has also done some fascinating research into
obesity, diabetes, insulin, because you reckon that insulin is actually a
neurotransmitter, it affects brain function.

Stephanie Amiel: Well, we are not the only people that reckon that, but certainly
we have a bit of evidence of that in the particular area of appetite control, which
is obviously of great interest to us because of the worries about the number of
people who are becoming insulin resistant, obese, and getting Type 2 diabetes.

Norman Swan: So you've flipped it on its head because you actually think for
some people what comes first in the pathway to diabetes is not obesity but it
actually is an insulin problem.

Stephanie Amiel: We have now some evidence for that. They have always been
very tightly linked, so people know that not for everybody but for most people
who are obese they are insulin resistant, most people with…

Norman Swan: Meaning insulin doesn't work as well.

Stephanie Amiel: Insulin doesn't work very well, exactly. And those people with
Type 2 are also insulin resistant. And so we've never really known which comes
first, but we've very recently done another brain imaging study in fact where we
took people who were insulin resistance, so they had very high insulin levels in
order to control their blood glucoses. So they've got normal glucose, they are not
diabetic, but they are using a lot of insulin or making a lot of insulin in order to
achieve that, and nor were they obese. Most of them weren't even overweight.
So they were apparently completely healthy people in whom the only pathology
we could find was that they were making more insulin to maintain normality than
someone who is more insulin sensitive.

And what we did was to compare their brain's response to eating with people
who were completely insulin sensitive. And we found some significant
differences. Strangely enough, again in these areas of the brain that control
appetite and pleasure and the areas of the brain also that inhibit our basic
instincts. So obviously the natural instincts of an animal like man is to eat
something, and we have frontal cortical control of that so that we don't just go on
eating forever. And the front parts of our brain control our ability to stop eating
and our ability not to eat again if we are not hungry.
 
And those brain areas appear to function differently in people who are not obese
and not diabetic but who are insulin resistant. We know those people are at high
risk for getting obesity and diabetes, and so it looks to us as though the insulin
resistance comes first, and it may be that in altering the way the brain responds
to food and alters the person's relationship to food, that may be why those people
then go on to develop obesity and diabetes.

Norman Swan: So how do you know that you're insulin resistant if you're not fat?

Stephanie Amiel: What we did was look for people who were at high risk for
being insulin resistant. So we looked for family members of people who had Type
2 diabetes.

Norman Swan: And you've also found that with bariatric surgery, people's
behaviour changes, there is something hormonal that goes on.

Stephanie Amiel: There is indeed. So we've known for a long time that bariatric
surgery doesn't just change how much you eat, it also changes what you eat and
your interest in eating.

Norman Swan: Just tell us more about that.

Stephanie Amiel: Well, there are different forms of bariatric surgery, but the one
that is probably most successful in weight control and improving diabetes is
something called gastric bypass. It's a fairly major procedure but it removes the
stomach and it bypasses the very first part of the small intestinal, so the food
goes straight from the gullet straight into the rest of the small intestinal.

Norman Swan: It's called Roux-en-Y…

Stephanie Amiel: It is indeed called Roux-en-Y, and it's very successful. And we
know that when that happens to you it doesn't just cause weight loss because of
restricting the amount you can eat physically, it's not malabsorptive, but it
changes your appetite control, it changes your taste for food, and it seems to
change the things you enjoy eating in a more healthy direction.

So we looked at people who had had that operation and who were weight stable
after it, and we again did some brain imaging studies looking at how their brains
responded to food intake. And we found that their brains responded differently
 
from the matched controls who were equally obese but hadn't had surgery. And
in some brain areas the surgery appeared to normalise what was an abnormal
response in the obese individual. And in other brain areas it seemed to
exaggerate or even invert the normal response, but all in ways that would be
expected to help the brain better control your food intake.

Norman Swan: It's absolutely astounding because what is happening in the gut
is having an effect in the brain.

Stephanie Amiel: Yes indeed, and there's a lot more knowledge about that now
because we understand a lot more about the signals that the gut generates when
you eat something. So the gut makes a series of proteins that go to the brain and
say this person has eaten, and that means you will stop eating because that
creates a signal that tells you to stop eating, and some of those signals also
control the length of time before you feel you need to eat again.

Norman Swan: And your food preference.

Stephanie Amiel: And your food preference, absolutely, it's all about appetite
control and pleasure and what seems good to you.

Norman Swan: And they are also taking more exercise.

Stephanie Amiel: I'm not sure how well that has been documented. We certainly
saw that in a recent very small study we did using a little device that mimics one
of the effects of the Roux-en-Y which is to exclude the duodenum, the upper part
of the small intestine. And with that device, where food didn't touch the top part of
the small intestine as it went through to the bowe…this is purely anecdotal, not
very scientific, but anecdotally those people not only changed what they ate and
how much they ate, they started to exercise. So that needs investigating because
that's very exciting.

Norman Swan: Stephanie Amiel is Professor of Diabetic Medicine at King's
College London.

One of the hot areas in cancer research at the moment is the idea of the liquid
biopsy. Sounds goopy I know but it is the hope that if you look closely enough at
a person's blood there may be a lot it can tell you, either about whether they have
 
cancer to begin with, or how effective a treatment might be. Francesco Grignani
is Professor of Pathology at the University of Perugia.

Francesco Grignani: When you have early-stage lung cancer you actually do
not know whether this cancer will relapse after surgery or if the patient is cured
by surgery. At the moment there are very few parameters to predict what would
happen in the future for these patients, and we are looking for markers which
would help in predicting the outcome of these patients, and we actually think that
we can find these parameters in the blood of the patients.

Norman Swan: So simply a blood test.

Francesco Grignani: For the patient it's just a blood test.

Norman Swan: And what you are particularly looking at are lung cancers.

Francesco Grignani: We are studying lung cancer in our lab, but many labs all
over the world are actually studying with the same approach different types of
cancers but which a prognosis can be made by drawing a little bit of blood and
measuring new molecular parameters in the blood.

Norman Swan: It's complicated, but these so-called cancer markers or
biomarkers in the blood are often fragments of RNA called micro RNAs. One of
the key functions of RNA is to read off the genetic code held on the DNA on our
chromosomes and transport the messages to factories within the cell which will
then read the RNA and manufacture the proteins that the code is designed to
produce. In cancer there are abnormal RNAs from the pathological processes
inside cancer cells, and they can spill out from the cells into the blood. Francesco
Grignani again:

Francesco Grignani: So measuring these RNAs could help us in predicting what
happens in a cancer patient.

Norman Swan: You talk about a simple blood test, but then presumably once it
gets to the lab, that gets fairly complicated to actually work out what these RNAs
are.

Francesco Grignani: Of course. For the patient it's a blood test, but for us it's
very complicated, but the techniques are developing. So we are now able to
 
collect many, many clinical samples and perform good analysis in very large
numbers of patients to reach significant results.

Norman Swan: So what you've done is you've taken people with relatively early-
stage lung cancer and measured these RNAs. And what have you found?

Francesco Grignani: Well, we found that a certain combination of these RNAs
suggests that the patient will relapse. And even a certain combination suggest
that a patient will die of his disease. On the other hand, if you do not have this
combination of RNAs, you are probably cured. So you will not need any further
therapy.

Norman Swan: Which is quite remarkable. And is this in smoking-related lung
cancer or non-smoking related lung cancer?

Francesco Grignani: This is actually even more solid in non-smoking-related
lung cancer. For smoking-related cancers, several groups are working on
predicting the onset of the cancer before it can be seen in imaging techniques by
looking at the blood of the people who are at risk of lung cancer.

Norman Swan: One of the problems with blood tests is reliability. How accurate
is the testing for these RNAs at the moment and how long before it becomes so
standardised that you can really do it reliably?

Francesco Grignani: The way you get the blood and the way you store the
blood is standardised. And probably in a few years will be routine.

Norman Swan: And the price? Because cost in Italy and in Australia is really
important.

Francesco Grignani: Now this is costly. But identifying a few of these RNAs…

Norman Swan: So it's cheaper when you know what you're looking…

Francesco Grignani: It's much cheaper if you measure three, four RNAs instead
of measuring a few hundred RNAs.

Norman Swan: The other question that patients will have is, well, it's fine telling
me…well, I don't want to hear it but it's fine telling me that I'm going to relapse or
 
I might even die, but are there any treatment insights that you can get from these
RNAs? Do they relate to the increasing number of genetic mutations which tell
you that a certain drug might work on your cancer?

Francesco Grignani: This is something we are looking at right now, and
hopefully we will find the correlation that we are looking for, for a better treatment
of the cancer.

Norman Swan: Francesco Grignani is Professor of Pathology at the University of
Perugia. And you've been listening to the Health Report with me, Norman Swan.
Look forward to your company next week.

pages.text:
Norman Swan: Hello, welcome to this week's edition of the Health Report with
me, Norman Swan. Today, time for a cold shower on the hype around medicinal
cannabis. Could Mars Bars protect against obesity? How obesity might not be
the main step on the road to diabetes. And the prospect that a blood test could
tell you as much about your cancer as a biopsy.

There's been a remarkable turnaround in attitudes and legislation making it
easier for people to take cannabis for medicinal purposes, and for the
manufacture of cannabis products for medical uses. But before we get carried
away, an editorial in this week's Medical Journal of Australia warns that there are
still significant gaps in knowledge which could put users at risk. One of the co-
authors of the editorial is Jennifer Martin, who is Professor of Clinical
Pharmacology at the University of Newcastle, and Jennifer was in our Newcastle
studio last night. Welcome to the Health Report.

Jennifer Martin: Thank you, I'm pleased to be here.

Norman Swan: You talk about that you still require data…we still don't know how
effective, how safe and what the dose range is of these cannabis products.

Jennifer Martin: That's correct. We need more data, but in addition we also
need a whole lot of other things to happen to make sure that we have actually
ensured that patients are safe when they take cannabis.

Norman Swan: So what are the worries? Are there any signals about worries at
the moment?

Jennifer Martin: I think there are a lot of concerns from prescribers, for example
they have concerns as to how they would write a script for cannabis, which type
of cannabis would they prescribe, how would they prefer to give it? Is it given in a
tablet or vaporised or smoked? What is the recommendation for this particular
patient with this particular disease? So I think there are concerns in the
profession about that aspect. I also think there are concerns in other areas that
maybe haven't had so much coverage such as the pharmacists who are going to
have to be sure they know how to store the cannabis and that all of the many
different cannabis products…they'll have to know how to look after them, what
the security is around them, how these things will be prescribed and what the
follow-up for patients is.

Norman Swan: Are there many products on the market yet? What's around at
the moment in Australia? I know there is a lot on the market in the United States.

Jennifer Martin: Yes, so it's still an illegal substance, that's the law. But patients
that I look after in the hospital are still able to access different types of cannabis
and cannabinoid from overseas, and many grow it actually at home in the Hunter
and make up their own products. So there is quite a market out there of people
that are already making or importing these therapeutic products to use
themselves medicinally.

Norman Swan: Have you seen anybody get into strife?

Jennifer Martin: I have actually seen quite a few people in strife. Most of them
actually it's after the event and we are talking about how to manage, for example,
their end-stage heart failure or their end-stage airways disease, and they tell me
about a bad experience they've had with cannabis that has been
prescribed…well, it's not prescribed, that has been brought to them by friends or
family members that are trying to be helpful. And these are a particular
population group that is often neglected in health, such as the elderly, and the
elderly patients, they describe quite significant cognitive and dysphoric reactions
after having cannabis.

Norman Swan: And if you are importing cannabis from overseas, do we know
what's in it?

Jennifer Martin: We don't know what's in it, that's correct. There are places that
you can get it tested. For example, at Newcastle University we have the facilities
to actually identify compounds that are actually within the cannabinoid product.
Most of them are THC, which is the hallucinogenic compound, and CBD which is
a cannabidiol which has been studied in epilepsy, but there are a variety of other
things that are in there and that are added to it. But that's correct, people
themselves actually wouldn't know that.

Norman Swan: Some people would say (and I can just see my mailbag
tomorrow morning), well, you know, these are just the old farts in the medical
profession trying to put up the barriers here and the best thing is just to smoke it,
all this medicinal stuff is just a smokescreen for pharmaceutical companies to
make a lot of money.

Jennifer Martin: Yes, that's exactly the feedback we get from some members of
the community as well, they are a bit frustrated that the trials are taking so long.
We haven't even started recruiting for some of them. We don't have an active
pharmacovigilance program out there, and people are saying, well, why are you
taking so long, we all know the stuff is good, why don't you just get on with it?
And I think for recreational users that's a reasonable argument because we do
have 2,000 years of information from people who use it recreationally.

But medicinal cannabis is used in a completely different group usually, it's usually
an older group, they are usually pretty frail and comorbid, that means they have
lots of other medical problems. They are on lots and lots of drugs that might
interact with the cannabis, they might have difficulty inhaling a particular form of
cannabis because they lack the ability to inhale to get the active ingredients.

So I think the group that we're getting a lot of pressure from is usually a
recreational group, and I think that what I'm concerned about as a medical
practitioner is more about protecting patients, about making sure we actually
don't give them something that's not safe and actually potentially harm them. I
actually think that's a reasonable…I mean, I understand what you're saying about
the paternalistic…well, potentially implying that this might be the paternalistic
view of medicine, but I do think we have a duty to protect patients as well. And
the other point I have is just that there is a bit of research to suggest that some of
these molecules in the cannabis are actually quite helpful, and if we get it wrong,
if we actually don't do the studies properly upfront and choose the wrong dose to
study, then we might think…

Norman Swan: You could spoil it.

Jennifer Martin: We could spoil it, and you never get a second chance to go
back on that, the energy is gone and people are onto something else. So I think it
was really not trying to be…

Norman Swan: So go slower to get it right.

Jennifer Martin: I think so, and put the time and investment upfront to do the
studies properly.

Norman Swan: Jennifer, thanks very much for joining us.

Jennifer Martin: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Jennifer Martin is Professor of Clinical Pharmacology at the
University of Newcastle.

And you're listening to the Health Report here on RN with me, Norman Swan.

Research published by Australian researchers in a prestigious international
journal could be interpreted as showing that eating confectionery protects against
obesity. Before you scream with delight and devour that bar of chocolate you've
been eyeing in the cupboard, there may be more to this story. Earlier today I
spoke to two of the authors from the Murdoch Children's Research Institute in
Melbourne, Constantine Gasser and Professor Melissa Wake.

Melissa, what's the context for this study?

Melissa Wake: We've been very interested in obesity for a long time, and I think
it is becoming fairly clear that we have kind of hit a wall. So after 15 years of
really trying with education and lifestyle advice et cetera, we haven't got very far.
And we really felt that we needed to go back a little bit and really start to try and
unpick some possible contributors to obesity and healthy weight. So that led to
Constantine looking at this under-researched area.

Norman Swan: Which is the influence of confectionery on obesity. So what did
you do, Constantine?

Constantine Gasser: We conducted a systematic review where we combined
the results of 19 studies from around the world to look at the association between
confectionery consumption and overweight and obesity in children and
adolescents.

Norman Swan: Confectionery defined as what?

Constantine Gasser: Candy and chocolates, but not including other types of
sweets and deserts. So we looked at confectionery and overweight and obesity
and found to our surprise people with higher intakes of confectionery were
actually slightly less likely to be overweight or obese.

Norman Swan: Where the studies consistently in that direction?

Constantine Gasser: So most of the studies were consistently in that direction.

Norman Swan: So it's absolutely counterintuitive. And before we jump to the
conclusion that we should all go out and chomp away at a Mars Bar to protect
ourselves against obesity, let's just assume a neutral position for the moment on
this finding. If the finding were to be real, what sort of risk reduction on obesity
did you get for confectionery use?

Constantine Gasser: We compared children in the highest versus the lowest to
our reference category of confectionery consumption in the studies, and this
differed across each of the studies, but we found that overall the odds or
likelihood of being overweight or obese was approximately 20% lower for
children in the highest compared to the lowest or a reference category of
consumption, and this was similar for both chocolate and non-chocolate
confectionery.

Norman Swan: So, Constantine, I can hear people rejoicing across the land. Do
you think the finding is real? Given that several studies have shown it and if we
were talking about a more neutral topic you'd have said, oh, this is it, signed,
sealed and delivered, factor X protects you against Y, no problem at all.

Constantine Gasser: Well, we think that there are a number of possible reasons
for these findings. Firstly, the possibilities that confectionery may be a small
aspect of the diet of these children and adolescents, so it may not be contributing
very much to their daily energy or sugar intake. For example, US data shows that
confectionery or candy in the US comprises approximately 5% of their sugar
intake compared to soft drinks and other sugar sweetened drinks, which
comprise approximately 30%.

However, another reason for these findings is that overweight or obese children
or adolescents or their parents may reduce their confectionery intake if they
believe that it's an easy target in order to combat overweight or obesity, so they
may be reducing their intake of these foods.

Norman Swan: So what you're saying here is obese people have artificially
lowered their confectionery rates to try and control their obesity, and therefore
people who are thinner look artificially as if they are in a higher group.

Constantine Gasser: Yes, or they may have also underreported their intake of
confectionery if they believe that it was socially desirable to be consuming less
confectionery for health outcomes such as obesity, and as a result this may have
been an explanation for some of the findings as well.

Norman Swan: But it also could be real, that once you've had a lolly or two or a
bit of chocolate, your appetite for other sugar and other high calorie foods is
lower, and therefore there is a trade-off which is beneficial.

Constantine Gasser: Yes, possibly because of sugar being lower in kilojoules
than fat, then this may have also been another possible explanation, meaning
that they may have had an increased sense of fullness and consumed less of
other foods. But we do need to also consider the quantities that are being
consumed and also the detrimental effect of confectionery on other health
outcomes such as tooth decay, for example because of the high sugar content.
So we are certainly not saying that we should be encouraging high intakes of
confectionery.

Norman Swan: So Melissa Wake, you were hoping to illuminate the literature on
obesity and diet, and all you succeeded in doing is confusing it even more.

Melissa Wake: Well, we think that we have come up with a really interesting
finding. It does seem likely that confectionery consumption is a fairly small part of
children's food intake today. We think that the culprits for obesity are likely to be
too much food, so large servings, uncontrolled snacks, second helpings et
cetera, and also the sorts of foods that kids are predominantly eating; sugary
drinks, but also foods that are high in fat and salt and sugar and processed
carbohydrates, and large in terms of portion size.

Norman Swan: So Health Report listeners across the land and indeed across
the world since we've got Canadian listeners, are looking in their cupboard
hungrily at that bar of chocolate. What should they do with it, Melissa?

Melissa Wake: Well, first they should make sure that it's dark chocolate. They
should encourage children to eat sparingly. Certainly we know that dark
chocolate does actually have some health benefits. It does increase satiety, it's
quite hard to overindulge in dark chocolate, and its high flavonoid content has
been shown to have health benefits such as lower blood pressure. So I would

say keep an open mind, eat sparingly, and if your child does eat confectionery,
steer them towards something that does have ancillary health benefits.

Norman Swan: Thank you both very much indeed for joining us on the Health
Report.

Melissa Wake: It's a pleasure.

Constantine Gasser: Thanks Norman.

Norman Swan: Melissa Wake and Constantine Gasser at the Murdoch
Children's Research Institute in Melbourne.

Speaking of sugar and obesity, there are about a million people with diabetes in
Australia, which includes around 130,000 with what's called type 1, that's the
insulin-dependent form and not related to obesity necessarily. We are among the
highest prevalence nations in the world, and one of the problems with diabetes
that doesn't get much attention is the risk of hypoglycaemia, dangerously low
levels of blood sugar. And worryingly, some people with diabetes lose their ability
to recognise when their blood sugar is plummeting. And one answer may be re-
teaching people to become scared.

A world authority on hypoglycaemia was in Melbourne a few days ago, which is
where I caught up with her. And as you'll also hear, Professor Stephanie Amiel of
Kings College London also has fascinating findings on which comes first in type 2
diabetes; obesity or problems with insulin. And also, surprising side-effects of
obesity surgery. But let's start with hypoglycaemia.

Stephanie Amiel: A hypoglycaemic attack is never pleasant. For most people
they are what we call mild, but the patient may not feel them as mild because
what happens is the blood sugar goes low, they have a stress response which is
symptomatic, so it feels unpleasant, but they also know what is happening so
they eat something and it stops. The problem is that sometimes, particularly in
people who have lost the ability to feel that hypoglycaemia like that, the first thing
that happens is confusion and cognitive impairment, so they never get the
opportunity to treat themselves, the blood glucose goes on falling, they become
confused, they may behave in an embarrassing or abnormal way, and they may

get into loss of consciousness and seizure. And so those severe hypoglycaemic
attacks are obviously really very distressing and very unpleasant.

Norman Swan: And that's what you are trying to prevent. If you've got lack of
awareness, there is a major issue.

Stephanie Amiel: Yes, if you have too many minor hypos, most people will then
lose their ability to recognise them, and therefore they are much more prone to
get a more severe hypo. So if you've got type 1 diabetes and you don't recognise
when your blood glucose dips below, let's say, about three millimole per litre…

Norman Swan: And just to give people a sense of that, you've got diabetes when
you're fasting blood sugar is at seven, so three is at the lower end.

Stephanie Amiel: Sure, so under three and people start to notice or other people
start to notice in them a slight slowing of brain function. And so if you are not
noticing your own hypoglycaemia at or around that sort of level, then your risk for
having one of these more severe episodes is much increased. And if you are a
type 1 diabetic, so totally insulin-dependent from the beginning, then not being
aware of your hypoglycaemia increases your risk of having a really bad episode
by about sixfold. And if you are on insulin and you are type 2 diabetic person,
then 17-fold. It's a big risk factor.

Norman Swan: That's huge.

Stephanie Amiel: It is huge.

Norman Swan: You've been working on how you restore that awareness.

Stephanie Amiel: Yes, for a long time. It's time we got there! You can restore
it…this is going to sound very circular, but you can restore it by avoiding
exposure to a plasma glucose or blood glucose of under three because basically
what happens is the brain gets used to whatever you show it. So if you show it a
lot of blood glucoses of under three it stops noticing and stops warning you about
it.

Norman Swan: And that can happen to people who are trying too hard to keep
their blood sugar down.

Stephanie Amiel: Yes, it can, and particularly people who are very, very
committed to being really tightly controlled. And healthcare professionals have
been very good at telling people what glucose level they should be under. We
haven't been so good at making sure they realise that there is also a lower limit
to normality which they should remain over.

Norman Swan: So how do you get people to put a stop?

Stephanie Amiel: The most successful thing is to train people to manage their
own insulin very physiologically, so we call it flexible intensified insulin therapy,
and that's usually successful, so that will restore awareness of hypoglycaemia to
just under half of people who have lost awareness, and it hugely reduces the risk
of severe hypoglycaemia in the type 1 diabetic population.

Norman Swan: And in the Type 2?

Stephanie Amiel: We haven't done so much in the Type 2 because it's not such
a big problem for the type 2s, and that's partly because most Type 2s, even when
they need insulin, do still have a bit of their own insulin, and it seems to be all
they need to protect themselves from severe hypoglycaemia. Also partly because
there are now used agents, new non-insulin agents available for people that don't
carry the same hypoglycaemia risk. So if someone with Type 2 is having
hypoglycaemia problems, it's usually a matter of changing them onto one of
these in newer therapies with lower hypoglycaemic potential. And if they are on
insulin, then their problems are the same as the type 1s and they can join that
program.

Norman Swan: And it has also been found that transplanting part of the
pancreas can help too, and also you've been looking at psychological therapies.

Stephanie Amiel: Yes, there is one step in between that which is the use of the
newer technologies of glucose sensing and insulin delivery…

Norman Swan: These are the pumps and so on.

Stephanie Amiel: Sure. Because transplantation, it works but it's obviously not
suitable for everybody, and it's certainly not available to everybody.

We've been looking at psychological issues for a variety of reasons. We looked
at the brain's response to hypoglycaemia in a very scientific way, we did brain
imaging, brain scanning, and found that people who were unaware of their
hypoglycaemia had very different brain responses to hypoglycaemia, including a
failure to generate a message to themselves that this was something really
unpleasant that they should avoid at all costs.

Norman Swan: So they had a low stress response?

Stephanie Amiel: They had a low stress response, so they didn't have the stress
response, they didn't have the symptoms, we expected that because they were
unaware, what we didn't expect was they had different responses of the brain
areas that tell us we are having fun, the reward areas. And instead of turning
those off and really knowing that this was unpleasant, they weren't doing that and
some of them were even activating those areas in the opposite direction.

Norman Swan: Is that because of the sort of person they were or because of the
diabetes?

Stephanie Amiel: That's an extremely good question. We are testing that at the
moment. We think it's just part of the whole syndrome of having induced a
tolerance, if you like, of hypoglycaemia because you've been exposed to it too
often. But it is possible that this particular part of the response in what we call the
frontal areas of the brain, that might be genetically programmed in an individual,
so it may be that these people are programmed to respond to a stress in a
particular way that makes them more vulnerable to developing this whole
problem of unawareness.

Norman Swan: So teach them to become scared.

Stephanie Amiel: Absolutely we need to teach them to become scared because
if you don't feel something it's not surprising that you don't worry about it. But if
we can teach them to become scared, they will then be able to access all the
other information they've been given that they should have been able to use
before to help them avoid hypoglycaemia.

Norman Swan: Now, your group has also done some fascinating research into
obesity, diabetes, insulin, because you reckon that insulin is actually a
neurotransmitter, it affects brain function.

Stephanie Amiel: Well, we are not the only people that reckon that, but certainly
we have a bit of evidence of that in the particular area of appetite control, which
is obviously of great interest to us because of the worries about the number of
people who are becoming insulin resistant, obese, and getting Type 2 diabetes.

Norman Swan: So you've flipped it on its head because you actually think for
some people what comes first in the pathway to diabetes is not obesity but it
actually is an insulin problem.

Stephanie Amiel: We have now some evidence for that. They have always been
very tightly linked, so people know that not for everybody but for most people
who are obese they are insulin resistant, most people with…

Norman Swan: Meaning insulin doesn't work as well.

Stephanie Amiel: Insulin doesn't work very well, exactly. And those people with
Type 2 are also insulin resistant. And so we've never really known which comes
first, but we've very recently done another brain imaging study in fact where we
took people who were insulin resistance, so they had very high insulin levels in
order to control their blood glucoses. So they've got normal glucose, they are not
diabetic, but they are using a lot of insulin or making a lot of insulin in order to
achieve that, and nor were they obese. Most of them weren't even overweight.
So they were apparently completely healthy people in whom the only pathology
we could find was that they were making more insulin to maintain normality than
someone who is more insulin sensitive.

And what we did was to compare their brain's response to eating with people
who were completely insulin sensitive. And we found some significant
differences. Strangely enough, again in these areas of the brain that control
appetite and pleasure and the areas of the brain also that inhibit our basic
instincts. So obviously the natural instincts of an animal like man is to eat
something, and we have frontal cortical control of that so that we don't just go on
eating forever. And the front parts of our brain control our ability to stop eating
and our ability not to eat again if we are not hungry.

And those brain areas appear to function differently in people who are not obese
and not diabetic but who are insulin resistant. We know those people are at high
risk for getting obesity and diabetes, and so it looks to us as though the insulin
resistance comes first, and it may be that in altering the way the brain responds
to food and alters the person's relationship to food, that may be why those people
then go on to develop obesity and diabetes.

Norman Swan: So how do you know that you're insulin resistant if you're not fat?

Stephanie Amiel: What we did was look for people who were at high risk for
being insulin resistant. So we looked for family members of people who had Type
2 diabetes.

Norman Swan: And you've also found that with bariatric surgery, people's
behaviour changes, there is something hormonal that goes on.

Stephanie Amiel: There is indeed. So we've known for a long time that bariatric
surgery doesn't just change how much you eat, it also changes what you eat and
your interest in eating.

Norman Swan: Just tell us more about that.

Stephanie Amiel: Well, there are different forms of bariatric surgery, but the one
that is probably most successful in weight control and improving diabetes is
something called gastric bypass. It's a fairly major procedure but it removes the
stomach and it bypasses the very first part of the small intestinal, so the food
goes straight from the gullet straight into the rest of the small intestinal.

Norman Swan: It's called Roux-en-Y…

Stephanie Amiel: It is indeed called Roux-en-Y, and it's very successful. And we
know that when that happens to you it doesn't just cause weight loss because of
restricting the amount you can eat physically, it's not malabsorptive, but it
changes your appetite control, it changes your taste for food, and it seems to
change the things you enjoy eating in a more healthy direction.

So we looked at people who had had that operation and who were weight stable
after it, and we again did some brain imaging studies looking at how their brains
responded to food intake. And we found that their brains responded differently

from the matched controls who were equally obese but hadn't had surgery. And
in some brain areas the surgery appeared to normalise what was an abnormal
response in the obese individual. And in other brain areas it seemed to
exaggerate or even invert the normal response, but all in ways that would be
expected to help the brain better control your food intake.

Norman Swan: It's absolutely astounding because what is happening in the gut
is having an effect in the brain.

Stephanie Amiel: Yes indeed, and there's a lot more knowledge about that now
because we understand a lot more about the signals that the gut generates when
you eat something. So the gut makes a series of proteins that go to the brain and
say this person has eaten, and that means you will stop eating because that
creates a signal that tells you to stop eating, and some of those signals also
control the length of time before you feel you need to eat again.

Norman Swan: And your food preference.

Stephanie Amiel: And your food preference, absolutely, it's all about appetite
control and pleasure and what seems good to you.

Norman Swan: And they are also taking more exercise.

Stephanie Amiel: I'm not sure how well that has been documented. We certainly
saw that in a recent very small study we did using a little device that mimics one
of the effects of the Roux-en-Y which is to exclude the duodenum, the upper part
of the small intestine. And with that device, where food didn't touch the top part of
the small intestine as it went through to the bowe…this is purely anecdotal, not
very scientific, but anecdotally those people not only changed what they ate and
how much they ate, they started to exercise. So that needs investigating because
that's very exciting.

Norman Swan: Stephanie Amiel is Professor of Diabetic Medicine at King's
College London.

One of the hot areas in cancer research at the moment is the idea of the liquid
biopsy. Sounds goopy I know but it is the hope that if you look closely enough at
a person's blood there may be a lot it can tell you, either about whether they have

cancer to begin with, or how effective a treatment might be. Francesco Grignani
is Professor of Pathology at the University of Perugia.

Francesco Grignani: When you have early-stage lung cancer you actually do
not know whether this cancer will relapse after surgery or if the patient is cured
by surgery. At the moment there are very few parameters to predict what would
happen in the future for these patients, and we are looking for markers which
would help in predicting the outcome of these patients, and we actually think that
we can find these parameters in the blood of the patients.

Norman Swan: So simply a blood test.

Francesco Grignani: For the patient it's just a blood test.

Norman Swan: And what you are particularly looking at are lung cancers.

Francesco Grignani: We are studying lung cancer in our lab, but many labs all
over the world are actually studying with the same approach different types of
cancers but which a prognosis can be made by drawing a little bit of blood and
measuring new molecular parameters in the blood.

Norman Swan: It's complicated, but these so-called cancer markers or
biomarkers in the blood are often fragments of RNA called micro RNAs. One of
the key functions of RNA is to read off the genetic code held on the DNA on our
chromosomes and transport the messages to factories within the cell which will
then read the RNA and manufacture the proteins that the code is designed to
produce. In cancer there are abnormal RNAs from the pathological processes
inside cancer cells, and they can spill out from the cells into the blood. Francesco
Grignani again:

Francesco Grignani: So measuring these RNAs could help us in predicting what
happens in a cancer patient.

Norman Swan: You talk about a simple blood test, but then presumably once it
gets to the lab, that gets fairly complicated to actually work out what these RNAs
are.

Francesco Grignani: Of course. For the patient it's a blood test, but for us it's
very complicated, but the techniques are developing. So we are now able to

collect many, many clinical samples and perform good analysis in very large
numbers of patients to reach significant results.

Norman Swan: So what you've done is you've taken people with relatively early-
stage lung cancer and measured these RNAs. And what have you found?

Francesco Grignani: Well, we found that a certain combination of these RNAs
suggests that the patient will relapse. And even a certain combination suggest
that a patient will die of his disease. On the other hand, if you do not have this
combination of RNAs, you are probably cured. So you will not need any further
therapy.

Norman Swan: Which is quite remarkable. And is this in smoking-related lung
cancer or non-smoking related lung cancer?

Francesco Grignani: This is actually even more solid in non-smoking-related
lung cancer. For smoking-related cancers, several groups are working on
predicting the onset of the cancer before it can be seen in imaging techniques by
looking at the blood of the people who are at risk of lung cancer.

Norman Swan: One of the problems with blood tests is reliability. How accurate
is the testing for these RNAs at the moment and how long before it becomes so
standardised that you can really do it reliably?

Francesco Grignani: The way you get the blood and the way you store the
blood is standardised. And probably in a few years will be routine.

Norman Swan: And the price? Because cost in Italy and in Australia is really
important.

Francesco Grignani: Now this is costly. But identifying a few of these RNAs…

Norman Swan: So it's cheaper when you know what you're looking…

Francesco Grignani: It's much cheaper if you measure three, four RNAs instead
of measuring a few hundred RNAs.

Norman Swan: The other question that patients will have is, well, it's fine telling
me…well, I don't want to hear it but it's fine telling me that I'm going to relapse or

I might even die, but are there any treatment insights that you can get from these
RNAs? Do they relate to the increasing number of genetic mutations which tell
you that a certain drug might work on your cancer?

Francesco Grignani: This is something we are looking at right now, and
hopefully we will find the correlation that we are looking for, for a better treatment
of the cancer.

Norman Swan: Francesco Grignani is Professor of Pathology at the University of
Perugia. And you've been listening to the Health Report with me, Norman Swan.
Look forward to your company next week.
